meta.title: Who really said "Survival of the fittest"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Herbert Spencer coined it in Principles of Biology (1864), five years after reading Darwin. Darwin only adopted it in 1868, and put it into On the Origin of Species with the fifth edition of 1869 — at Alfred Russel Wallace's urging.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Survival of the fittest'?
meta.ogDescription: Spencer coined it in 1864. Darwin liked it, borrowed it in 1868 and added it to the Origin in 1869 — and the borrowing quietly changed what the phrase means.

answer.label: Coined by Herbert Spencer, 1864 — borrowed by Darwin in 1869
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine ‘both, sort of’ case. The phrase was coined by Herbert Spencer in The Principles of Biology, volume 1 (1864), page 444, written after he had read On the Origin of Species. Darwin did not use it in the first four editions of the Origin. He adopted it in The Variation of Animals and Plants Under Domestication in 1868, and folded it into the fifth edition of the Origin in 1869, in Chapter IV. So Darwin really did say it — ten years late, and crediting Spencer by name every time.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: This survival of the fittest, which I have here sought to express in mechanical terms, is that which Mr. Darwin has called ‘natural selection’, or the preservation of favoured races in the struggle for life.
trail: Spencer’s sentence is the origin point, and note what it is doing: he is not proposing a rival theory, he is offering Darwin a better phrase. It appears in The Principles of Biology, volume 1, page 444, published in 1864 the page ↗.

The bridge is Alfred Russel Wallace. In July 1866 he wrote to Darwin arguing that ‘natural selection’ made readers imagine nature consciously choosing, and that Spencer’s term avoided the trap. Darwin replied on 5 July 1866 that the letter was ‘as clear as daylight,’ called it ‘H. Spencer’s excellent expression’ — then objected that, grammatically, it cannot govern a verb Darwin Correspondence Project ↗.

Darwin used it in print for the first time in The Variation of Animals and Plants Under Domestication (1868), p. 6, and in 1869 changed the Chapter IV heading of the Origin to ‘Natural Selection; or the Survival of the Fittest.’ The sentence on pages 91–92 of that fifth edition reads: ‘This preservation of favourable variations, and the destruction of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection, or the Survival of the Fittest’ the 1869 page ↗.
source.excerptNote: Spencer’s original, and the whole argument is in the word ‘mechanical.’ He wanted evolution restated as physics — forces, equilibrium, no chooser anywhere. That is also why the phrase is so easy to misuse: strip the mechanics and it sounds like a moral verdict on who deserves to survive.

source.rightsNote: Both texts are long out of copyright. Spencer died in 1903 and the Principles of Biology was published in 1864; Darwin died in 1882 and the fifth edition of the Origin appeared in 1869. Quote either freely. Modern scholarly editions carry their own editorial apparatus — introductions, notes, annotations — which is not free, but the 19th-century sentences themselves are. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Charles Darwin
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Darwin
author.metaLine: 1809–1882 · English naturalist, author of On the Origin of Species
author.bio: Charles Darwin gets the credit because the phrase now works as a four-word summary of his book, and because he really did put it in that book — just not until the fifth edition, a decade after the first. He was scrupulous about the borrowing, writing in 1868 that ‘Mr. Herbert Spencer has well expressed the same idea by the Survival of the Fittest,’ and adding to the Origin’s introduction that Spencer’s expression ‘is more accurate, and is sometimes equally convenient.’ He was also uneasy about it: it cannot be used as a verb, and it invites exactly the misreading it was meant to prevent.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Nobody is lying here, which is what makes it interesting. Darwin did say it, in a book everyone has heard of. He just did not think of it, and the ten-year gap between the coinage and the borrowing is where the meaning went sideways.

items.why: The phrase is absent from the first four editions of the Origin (1859, 1860, 1861, 1866). It arrives in 1869, in Chapter IV of the fifth edition, five years after Spencer printed it and always with Spencer credited by name.

The Principles of Biology, vol. 1, p. 444. Spencer had sketched a related idea in his 1852 essay ‘A Theory of Population,’ but the words themselves date from 1864, and he wrote them after reading Darwin — so the coinage is downstream of the theory, not the other way round.

Wallace pressed the swap on Darwin in July 1866, arguing that ‘natural selection’ made readers picture nature consciously selecting. Darwin agreed the point was ‘as clear as daylight’ but complained that the phrase cannot be used as a substantive governing a verb — a grammarian’s objection that turned out to matter less than the marketing the correspondence ↗.

For Darwin, ‘fittest’ meant best matched to an immediate local environment — think of a puzzle piece, not an athlete. Spencer, an economist and social theorist first, was drawing a deliberate parallel with his own theories of competition, and it is his reading that survives in everyday use.

misattribution.truthLine: Herbert Spencer coined it in The Principles of Biology in 1864; Darwin borrowed it in 1868 and added it to the Origin in 1869, crediting Spencer each time the trail ↗.

context.heading: Why the distinction matters
lead: Whose phrase it is turns out to decide what it means. In Darwin’s hands it is a description: organisms that happen to suit their surroundings leave more offspring, and nothing is choosing anybody. In Spencer’s hands it is already halfway to an argument about society, because Spencer arrived at it while drawing parallels between biology and his own economics.

That is why the phrase became the banner of social Darwinism — a movement named after the man who did not coin the phrase and did not make the argument. If you want the sentence that carries Darwin’s actual claim, it is the clumsier one: ‘natural selection.’
detailsBody: 1859: On the Origin of Species, first edition. The phrase does not appear.
1864: Spencer, The Principles of Biology, vol. 1, p. 444 — the coinage, explicitly offered as a restatement of Darwin.
July 1866: Wallace writes to Darwin urging the swap; Darwin calls the argument ‘as clear as daylight’ and the expression ‘excellent,’ but notes it is grammatically awkward.
1868: Darwin uses it in print for the first time, in Variation, p. 6.
1869: Fifth edition of the Origin. Chapter IV becomes ‘Natural Selection; or the Survival of the Fittest.’
context.pull: Darwin meant 'best matched to right here, right now'. Think of a puzzle piece, not an athlete.
